newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk bankers urge concrete govt steps on economy.
newsitem.headline: Turk bankers urge concrete govt steps on economy.

text.p: Turkey's new coalition government is apparently set to focus on short-term economic measures rather than tackle the economy's deep-seated structural problems, bankers said.
Bankers said they supported the economic targets set out in the government programme this week, but said concrete action was vital to put the plans into practice.
Conservative Yilmaz, appointed prime minister last month at the head of a secularist government, said in a speech to parliament on Monday that he would give a high priority to reducing inflation.
He promised that his coalition, formed with the goal of putting an end to months of political chaos, would speed up privatisation. "Work on selling state banks will be increased," he said.
But the programme did not address the need for far-reaching economic reforms ahead of early elections expected by mid-1998, bankers said.

"The programme of the three-party coalition government does not include radical measures to overcome the economy's structural problems," said Sukru Karahasanoglu, president of Sumerbank, Turkey's first privatised state bank.

"But it is clear that the government aims to concentrate on fundamental measures," he told Reuters. He said bankers and the markets would support any postive steps on basic problems such as annual inflation around 75 percent and unstable public finances.
Karahasanoglu said he believed the government was sincere on selling state banks. A view shared by other bankers.
"We appreciate the government's promise to increase work on selling state banks," Nadir Topcuoglu, general manager of private Yasarbank, told Reuters.
"But it is very hard to realise this target because of their immense structures," he added.
Topcuoglu said selling off public banks would made easier if their growth was curbed, or they were slimmed down. He pointed in particular to advertising campaigns as a major expense.
"If they are to be privatised why do they still have advertisement campaigns with large budgets," he asked.
Topcuoglu said the overall privatisation of state banks would be made easier if some services, such as tax collection, were also sold off.
